question: A small-cap Indian textile company reports rising Net Profit for three consecutive years, but its Cash Flow from Operations has been negative each year. As an analyst, what is the most likely concern?
before: This pattern — rising profits with persistently negative CFO — is one of the most reliable forensic accounting red flags in the Indian small-cap and mid-cap space. It often signals: (1) Aggressive revenue recognition (booking sales that have not actually happened or are not collectible), (2) Receivables ballooning faster than sales (customers not paying, but revenue is still recorded), (3) Inventory build-up being capitalised rather than expensed, or (4) Outright fraud. Several Indian corporate scandals — including Satyam and various delisted SME stocks — showed exactly this pattern before unravelling. Option A is wrong: even high-growth companies should show CFO trending toward positive over time; persistent negative CFO with rising profits is not "normal". Option C is wrong and irrelevant — issuing equity does not fix earnings quality issues. Option D is wrong because tax overpayment would not cause this divergence pattern. The lesson: always cross-check Net Profit against CFO. We will go much deeper into this in Module 8 (Red Flag Analysis).
after:
Concept: Earnings quality is the degree to which reported net profit reflects actual economic cash generation. A persistent divergence between rising net profit and negative operating cash flow signals that profits may not be backed by real cash inflows — a fundamental red flag in equity analysis.

Why this is correct: When net profit rises but cash flow from operations remains negative year after year, the company is reporting accounting earnings that are not converting to cash. This almost always points to one of three problems: aggressive revenue recognition (recording sales before payment is assured), growing receivables that customers are not settling, or inventory being capitalized rather than expensed. This is not a tax issue, a growth phase excuse, or an equity problem — it is a quality-of-earnings problem that signals either aggressive accounting or deteriorating customer payment discipline. Indian small-cap fraud cases (Satyam, delisted SME boards) typically show this exact pattern months before collapse.

Why the others are wrong: Option A misunderstands growth company dynamics. Even rapid-growth companies should show operating cash flow trending toward positive as revenues mature; persistent negative CFO with rising profits is never normal and indicates the profit growth is not real. Option C is irrelevant because issuing more equity does not cure earnings quality problems — it masks them temporarily and distracts from the root issue of whether profits are genuine. Option D is incorrect because excess tax payments would reduce net profit, not inflate it; they have no bearing on the CFO-to-NP divergence pattern.

Intuition: Net profit is an accounting construct vulnerable to timing and judgment calls; operating cash flow is harder to manipulate because it is based on actual cash movement. When they diverge sharply and persistently, always suspect the accruals (revenue recognition, receivables, inventory) are doing the heavy lifting of reported profit growth. This is the first place an analyst should look when a small-cap's topline looks too good to be true.
